title: Every Tear That Flows from an Eye Has a Cause
intro: The Diwan places this poem in Sarandib, now Sri Lanka, where al-Barudi was exiled after the Urabi revolt in Egypt. Lightning on a distant horizon summons a valley, its inhabitants and a woman walking among her companions. When the poet finally names his exile, the lover’s remonstrance opens into a defence of his conduct and a hope that political fortunes, too, can change.

translation: Every tear that flows from an eye has a cause.
How could a grieving man hold back his tears?
1.sharh: His first claim is deliberately general. Abdallah al-Tayyib hears an echo of al-Busiri’s Burda in the phrase about a tear running from an eye. The cause particular to this man emerges much later.

translation: Without the struggle against longing no eye would weep,
no heart beat wildly through the night.
2.sharh: The eye offers a sign a bystander can see. The beating heart carries the same argument into the hidden hours when there is nobody there to witness it.

translation: You who blame me, spare me a hasty reproach.
Love is a ruler who has the upper hand.
3.sharh: The reproacher is addressed familiarly, as someone with whom he might reason. The first ruler named in this poem of political exile is love, whose commands the speaker knows from within.

translation: Had a man a mind to light his way
through the darkness of doubt, calamities would never fasten on him.
4.sharh: The rebuke assumes disasters could have been foreseen. He gives that assumption a physical test by imagining a lamp that would have had to shine into doubt beforehand.

translation: Could he make out what is still hidden of events,
he would know what to undertake and what to avoid.
5.sharh: Taking a step and withholding it would both be easy with advance knowledge. The two verbs expose the advantage enjoyed by anyone judging a decision after its outcome is known.

translation: Instead he stands a target for time to shoot at
with arrows that have neither feathers nor sinew.
6.sharh: Feathers steady an arrow, and sinew belongs to the archer’s equipment. Time’s shafts arrive without the familiar signs of an approaching shot.

translation: How can I hide my longing when a passion in me
nearly splits my insides at its touch?
7.sharh: The poem has been reasoning in the abstract. A mere touch now threatens to tear apart the speaker’s body, bringing the argument back to the effort of hiding tears.

translation: How can I forget, with a heart that almost flames
whenever lightning flares on the horizon?
8.sharh: A flash far beyond the speaker seems to ignite an answering fire inside him. Al-Tayyib connected the storm imagery with the poet’s experience of lightning in Sarandib.

translation: In love I have folded myself around such burning pains
that even the mildest all but catches at my soul.
9.sharh: The folded body suggests a fire kept under wraps. If the mildest ember can catch at life itself, the stronger ones need no description.

translation: When I breathe out, my sigh spills sparks,
as flame springs bright behind a stroke of the firestone.
10.sharh: A sigh lets the fire of the last verse escape. “Behind” gives the order of the familiar event, the strike first and the flame close upon it.

translation: I have nothing left to give but my own life.
I have given that. Is there mercy due me now?
11.sharh: The second half quietly completes the sacrifice announced in the first. Only after the account is empty does the speaker put in a claim for compassion.

translation: When passion rises in my heart, it is
a bird thrashing in a trap inside my ribs.
12.sharh: The bird’s attempts to escape make its confinement more visible. Ribs supply a second enclosure around the trap, bringing the old image close to the speaker’s own pulse.

translation: Love gives my heart no respite from its searing pains,
as if my heart and desire were blood relations.
13.sharh: Kinship usually explains solicitude or attachment. Here it explains why something so hurtful can nevertheless lay permanent claim to the heart.

translation: Do not blame me for the tears that ran down
the slope of al-Aqiq. I have business in their flowing.
14.sharh: The second safh can refer back to the hillside or mean the shedding of tears. Both the Diwan’s editors and al-Tayyib hear the two possibilities, a destination and a release.

translation: Those homes, whenever their outlines appear
on the page of my mind, stir me to the depths.
15.sharh: A mental page replaces the physical landscape. Tarab can be a violent stirring produced by grief as readily as by joy, which matters when a recollection briefly seems so vivid.

translation: I pledged myself to their inhabitants, to my sorrow.
A pledge breaks when affection fails to guard it.
16.sharh: His own fidelity has made him vulnerable. A formal undertaking has no life in separation unless affection continues to sustain it.

translation: My trust, once sound, has sickened.
A judgment sometimes falls wide, sometimes comes close.
17.sharh: Confidence has a body that can fall ill. In the second half a guess is measured by its distance from the truth, leaving some uncertainty even in his disappointment.

translation: Lords of the protected ground, what has become of your help?
It comes so scantily, and you men so nobly born.
18.sharh: A hima is ground under protection. Addressing its chiefs by that title makes a pointed claim on precisely the service from which he now feels excluded.

translation: You left me to my fate when I had trusted you.
Arabs, since when have you broken pledged protection?
19.sharh: The audience widens from local chiefs to “Arabs.” The ground of his complaint is an existing bond, one on which he had relied before his hardship began.

translation: Should not the stranger lodging among you find
safety when he fears destruction drawing near?
20.sharh: A guest who has taken shelter can claim protection as of right. It is the approach of danger that turns an ordinary courtesy into a test of the host.

translation: How then, with no injury to avenge, can she steal my heart,
a girl behind a curtain, a kinswoman of this camp?
21.sharh: A blood claim might justify retaliation between clans. He plays at bringing a claim against a woman of his hosts’ own kin for the wholly unprovoked theft of his heart.

translation: She passed us walking slowly among her friends,
a full moon in a halo ringed with stars.
22.sharh: The slow walk lets the eye arrange the women into a moving constellation. The halo keeps the group together while its centre stands out.

translation: She sways, long tresses over silk,
like a straight spear tasselled with lilies.
23.sharh: Silken clothing and full hair give the erect figure both texture and motion. The lilies are imagined as the spear’s tassels, moving although the shaft remains straight.

translation: Her forehead, just beneath the fringe,
is dawn still veiled by a departing darkness.
24.sharh: The dark fringe makes a veil for the brightness of the forehead. Dawn is caught before the last of night has drawn fully back.

translation: She was to us a sign of beauty, then she vanished
into separation’s night. Even the full moon goes out of sight.
25.sharh: The earlier moon simile can now account for disappearance as well as splendour. Familiarity with the moon’s return makes the comparison hopeful without promising her return.

translation: Could I have one glance to sustain my last breath,
some way my soul might seek, some means?
26.sharh: All he requests now is one look, enough for what remains of a life. The return of sabab, “means” or “cause,” quietly recalls the cause asserted in the first line.

translation: I pass the night in exile. My soul takes no ease
in it, and a meeting with my people is far off.
27.sharh: Exile has waited twenty-seven verses to be named. The unreachable company includes followers and friends, bringing the absent landscape into his political and personal life.

translation: No companion whose face would lift my spirits,
no friend to see what ails me and grieve.
28.sharh: He wants two kinds of company, the sight of a familiar face and someone willing to share sorrow. The last verb gives a friend the very condition that the opening assigned to the speaker.

translation: Among the wonders I have met with in my time
is this affliction, itself a wonder,
29.sharh: The verse withholds the substance of the case. The repetition of “wonder” gives the experience the continuing strangeness of a sentence whose grounds have never been explained.

translation: I committed no offence to bring about
this plight of mine. Why this misery and dispossession?
30.sharh: Harab can name the fury his treatment provokes. It can also name what exile cost him. Three verses later he recalls what the hands of misfortune took from him, lending weight to that second sense.

translation: Can my defence of my faith and my country
be a crime for which I am unjustly sentenced and exiled?
31.sharh: The charge and the defence finally confront each other in the same line. The exile speaks in his own political vocabulary, claiming the right to say what his act meant.

translation: Let no envious man suspect regret in me.
I bear it for God and look to Him for my reward.
32.sharh: The tears with which he began do not amount to a retraction. Ihtisab places the reckoning of his actions and their reward with God.

translation: I grew rich in honour. I took little heed
of what misfortune’s hands stripped away. That can be earned again.
33.sharh: Riches and gain belong to the language of property, but here the lasting asset is honour. The final pronoun points to the material things that can be acquired again.

translation: Want cannot bring down a soul that stands high.
Wealth cannot make an obscure man’s name resound.
34.sharh: Both halves test the supposed exchange rate between wealth and standing. Loss leaves one person’s worth intact, while accumulation cannot buy a name for another.

translation: I am a man whose first impulse fear cannot turn,
whose character anger cannot bend unjustly.
35.sharh: Quick action could look like rashness. The second half supplies the limit he claims for his courage, the ability to feel anger without letting it wrong somebody.

translation: I governed my temper and uttered nothing shameful.
I guarded my honour, and no suspicion took hold of it.
36.sharh: A word that would make its speaker blush never leaves his mouth. The man who earlier felt ruled by emotion can still claim mastery over public speech and conduct.

translation: I care little, with my conscience clear,
if people invent stories, however falsely they speak.
37.sharh: The repeated language of fabrication prepares an example in which a lie had what looked like physical evidence behind it.

translation: It is a slander, the very one once borne
by the lying blood on Joseph’s shirt, long before me.
38.sharh: In Qur’an 12 the brothers stain Joseph’s shirt to support their false story. Calling the blood itself a liar makes the false evidence, rather than Joseph, the distant counterpart of the charge against the poet.

translation: If my time has dealt ill with me and left me
in exile, without a brother to care for me,
39.sharh: Brotherhood here means someone who bends towards another with care. The conditional suspends the speaker’s present abandonment until the last verse can answer it.

translation: the nights will clear when their murk has passed.
Every cycle turns once it has run its course.
40.sharh: Change has hitherto worked against him. The fact that no turn of fortune lasts can now sustain hope, and the clearing night answers several earlier images of darkness.

2.1.2.head: مُكابَدَة
2.1.2.meaning: Struggling with something that takes sustained effort.

2.2.7.head: وَجَبَ
2.2.7.meaning: To throb or beat hard, here of the heart.

4.2.7.head: النُّوَب
4.2.7.meaning: Calamities that visit a person in their turn.

6.1.2.head: غَرَض
6.1.2.meaning: A mark set up for an archer to shoot at.

6.2.6.head: عَقَب
6.2.6.meaning: Sinew used for binding or making a bowstring.

7.1.5.head: كَلَف
7.1.5.meaning: An infatuation that burdens its bearer.

8.1.3.head: سَلا
8.1.3.meaning: To grow less troubled by the loss of someone one loves. A flash of lightning is enough to undo that relief.

9.1.2-3.head: في الحُبّ
9.1.2-3.meaning: In love, the condition in which he carries this burning pain. Both editions read fi al-hubb. The sung words can also be heard as bil-hubb, “through love”.

9.1.6.head: حُرقَة
9.1.6.meaning: Burning pangs of grief or longing. Even the gentlest of these pains almost seizes his soul.

9.2.4.head: اِنتَشَبَ
9.2.4.meaning: To catch hold and remain fastened.

10.2.4.head: القَدحَة
10.2.4.meaning: A single stroke made to strike fire.

14.1.6.meaning: “Down” or “on”, governing the slope named after the break. The sound at the pause resembles bi. The diwan and studio caption give fi.

14.2.1.head: سَفح
14.2.1.meaning: A slope. The same word can suggest pouring tears when it returns later in the half.

14.2.2.head: العَقيق
14.2.2.meaning: Al-Aqiq, a valley name used here for the beloved’s country.

14.2.6.head: أَرَب
14.2.6.meaning: A particular need or object of desire.

15.1.4.head: مَخايِل
15.1.4.meaning: Outlines or images presenting themselves to the mind.

18.1.2.head: سَراة
18.1.2.meaning: The leading men of a community.

18.1.3.meaning: Hima, ground reserved and defended by its people.

19.2.2.head: خَفَرَ
19.2.2.meaning: To violate a pledge of protection.

19.2.3-4.head: ذِمام العَهد
19.2.3-4.meaning: “The protection pledged”, the obligation one incurs by giving one’s word.

20.1.6.head: النَّزيل
20.1.6.meaning: A guest lodging under a community’s protection.

20.2.6.head: العَطَب
20.2.6.meaning: Ruin or death. The stranger seeks shelter because his life is at risk.

21.1.5.head: تِرَة
21.1.5.meaning: An earlier injury that gives rise to a claim for vengeance.

21.2.2.head: خِدر
21.2.2.meaning: A curtain enclosing a woman’s private quarters, and by extension the part of the dwelling behind it.

22.1.3.meaning: To move at an easy, swaying pace.

23.1.4.head: الفَينان
23.1.4.meaning: Full, luxuriant and long, of hair.

23.1.6.head: سَرَق
23.1.6.meaning: Saraq, fine silk or lengths of silk.

23.2.1.head: سَمهَرِيّ
23.2.1.meaning: Samhari, a fine straight spear. Here its shaft gives the woman her silhouette.

23.2.5.head: عَذَب
23.2.5.meaning: Hanging ends or tassels, here made of lilies.

24.1.2.head: غُرَّة
24.1.2.meaning: The bright forehead that shows beneath her hair. Its light gives rise to the image of daybreak.

24.1.5.head: طُرَّة
24.1.5.meaning: The fringe of hair falling over the forehead.

24.2.2.head: جانِحَة
24.2.2.meaning: Slanting away or departing, used of the darkness that veils first light.

25.2.3.meaning: Separation or distance, made into a night that hides a face.

27.2.5.head: شيعَة
27.2.5.meaning: One’s company of friends, followers or supporters.

29.2.2-3.head: مُنِيَ بِخَطب
29.2.2-3.meaning: “I was struck by a calamity.” The misfortune is the exile he described two verses earlier.

30.2.5.head: الحَرَب
30.2.5.meaning: Harab is the loss of one’s property. The verb hariba can also mean to grow intensely angry, the sense the diwan’s annotator gives here.

32.1.5.head: مَندَمَة
32.1.5.meaning: A feeling of regret, here an emotion his detractors would like to attribute to him.

32.2.5.head: مُحتَسِب
32.2.5.meaning: Bearing something in the hope of a reward from God.

35.1.6.head: بادِرَة
35.1.6.meaning: The first surge of resolve or impetuosity.

35.2.2.head: حافَ
35.2.2.meaning: To act unjustly. He refuses to let anger make him depart from his usual sense of fairness.

36.1.5.head: مَندِيَة
36.1.5.meaning: A disgraceful utterance that would bring a blush to the brow.

37.2.2.meaning: To invent a story or assert it without knowledge.

38.1.6.meaning: To come away bearing something and its consequences. The blood carries the fabricated charge.

38.2.6-7.head: دَم كَذِب
38.2.6-7.meaning: “Lying blood”, the fabricated evidence on Joseph’s shirt in Qur’an 12.18.

39.2.7.head: حَدِب
39.2.7.meaning: One who is solicitous and bends to another’s need.
